The Tacazze sunbird (Nectarinia tacazze) exhibits a relatively rapid early development when incubated under the thermal conditions typical of its highland nesting environment. Eggs maintained at a constant temperature of 33 °C [T = 33 °C] complete incubation in approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days], a developmental period that aligns well with the 14 to 17 day range documented for other medium-sized nectarivores at similar elevations. At the moment of hatching, the newly emerged altricial nestlings weigh just 1.88 grams [Ww0 = 1.88 grams], a remarkably low neonatal mass that underscores the extreme altriciality of this species. This initial mass is among the lightest recorded for any sunbird, reflecting the limited yolk reserves available at oviposition and the heavy reliance on immediate parental provisioning. The hatchlings are entirely naked and blind, requiring continuous brooding by the female to maintain body temperature during the first several days post-hatching. Such a small starting size imposes a steep energetic challenge for the parents, who must shuttle frequently between foraging grounds and the nest to meet the metabolic demands of their growing brood.

Under the ambient temperature regime typical of the active foraging season for this species, specifically at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the nestlings undergo a rapid developmental trajectory that culminates in fledging after 19 days since birth [tx = 19 days since birth]. This fledging interval is remarkably short for a passerine of this body size, reflecting the high predation pressure characteristic of its East African montane scrub habitat. The pin-feathered chicks develop their flight feathers quickly and achieve a body mass that approaches adult levels by the time of nest departure. Following this initial milestone, the young birds enter a period of gonadal quiescence that lasts until they reach sexual maturity. The time since birth at puberty has been documented at 57 days [tp = 57 days] at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a surprisingly early onset of reproductive capability that allows individuals hatched early in the breeding season to contribute to that same season's reproductive output. This accelerated maturation likely represents an adaptive response to the short and unpredictable rainfall patterns that define resource availability in its alpine environment.

Field records indicate that during the active metabolic phase, when body temperatures are maintained at approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the basal oxygen consumption of adult Tacazze sunbirds reaches 44 milliliters per hour [JOi = 44 milliliters per hour]. This resting metabolic rate is relatively elevated compared to other nectarivorous birds of similar mass, a pattern likely driven by the high energetic costs of hovering flight and the thermoregulatory demands of living at altitudes exceeding 2,500 meters. Fat stores are depleted rapidly during periods of inclement weather, and individuals may lose up to 15 percent of their body mass overnight if nectar availability is low. The species' physiological capacity to sustain such a high metabolic throughput on a sugar-rich diet is facilitated by extremely efficient intestinal disaccharidase activity, an adaptation shared with other specialized nectar-feeders. This metabolic intensity also influences the timing of first breeding, which does not occur until the birds have fully completed their somatic growth and attained their definitive adult plumage.

Sexual size dimorphism is evident in the asymptotic body masses attained by adult Tacazze sunbirds once growth is complete. Females reach an ultimate wet weight of 14.1 grams [Wwi = 14.1 grams], while males are conspicuously heavier at 15.7 grams [Wwi = 15.7 grams], a difference of roughly 11 percent that is typical for sunbird species exhibiting resource-defense polygyny. This dimorphism likely arises from the benefits of larger body size during male-male combat for high-quality feeding territories, which in turn attract visiting females. The larger male mass imposes a higher daily energy requirement, particularly during the breeding season when males must simultaneously defend their territory and engage in elaborate courtship displays. Despite the mass difference, both sexes share similar wing loading values, suggesting that the larger males compensate with proportionally longer wings. The attainment of these adult masses is generally complete within the first three months after hatching, after which the birds shift their energetic investment entirely toward reproduction and survival.

Reproductive output in the Tacazze sunbird follows a pattern typical of tropical highland passerines, characterized by moderate clutch sizes and multiple breeding attempts within a single season. When environmental conditions are favorable and body temperatures remain near 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], females lay 1 to 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 2 eggs per clutch] and produce up to 5 clutches per year [F_R_i = up to 5 clutches per year]. The relatively small clutch size is balanced by the frequency of nesting attempts, allowing females to spread reproductive risk across the protracted breeding season. The time since birth at first brood initiation is 438 days since birth [tR = 438 days since birth] under these thermal conditions, indicating that most individuals defer their first reproductive attempt until the second calendar year after hatching at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].
